title: Feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary outcomes of blended modality online parent training in exposure and response-prevention (ERP) for children with OCD.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study evaluated the co-design, feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary outcomes of a brief, intensive, parent-led cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention (CBT-ERP) intervention delivered via a blended digital modality.
METHOD: An open pilot case series (N = 4) involved families of children aged 7-14 years diagnosed with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The intervention comprised four self-guided web-based modules, four therapist-led videoconference group sessions, and a three-week maintenance phase with brief therapist check-ins. Feasibility was assessed through adherence, acceptability through usability, satisfaction, and recommendation ratings, and preliminary outcomes through clinician-, parent-, and child-reported OCD severity. .
RESULTS: Findings indicated high feasibility and acceptability, with strong intervention adherence and usability ratings within the "best imaginable" range. Parents reported high satisfaction, particularly with therapist-led sessions. OCD symptom severity decreased across measures, with 50% of participants no longer meeting diagnostic criteria at post-treatment, although changes were not statistically significant. Family accommodation remained relatively stable.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings provide preliminary support for the feasibility and acceptability of blended, parent-led CBT-ERP as a potentially scalable intervention for paediatric OCD. However, the small sample and uncontrolled design warrant cautious interpretation and further evaluation in larger controlled trials.
